extracted.intended_audience: naturalists, geologists, and educated readers interested in evolution and paleontology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for interpreting the fossil record, patterns of extinction and origination, and affinities among extinct and living species in support of descent with modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors affecting rate of modification
rubrics_metrics.description: The accumulation of variations and the amount of modification in species "depends on many complex contingencies,—on the variability being of a beneficial nature, on the power of intercrossing, on the rate of breeding, on the slowly changing physical conditions of the country, and more especially on the nature of the other inhabitants with which the varying species comes into competition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging expected rates of evolutionary change, consider whether variation is beneficial, the species' mating system and breeding rate, slow environmental change, and biotic interactions/competition. These factors explain why some species change faster or slower than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition and modification
rubrics_metrics.description: A form which does not become in some degree modified and improved "will be liable to be exterminated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret persistence or extinction of species in light of competition: lack of adaptive modification predicts replacement by improved competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological formations are intermittent samples
rubrics_metrics.description: Each formation "does not mark a new and complete act of creation, but only an occasional scene, taken almost at hazard, in a slowly changing drama."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat successive formations as continuous, complete records; expect wide and irregularly intermittent deposition, sampling gaps, and that apparent abrupt appearances/disappearances may be artefacts of incomplete strata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreversibility of identical reappearance
rubrics_metrics.description: A species when once lost should never reappear identically, because even if a new variety fills the same place it will "not be identically the same; for both would almost certainly inherit different characters from their distinct progenitors."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims of re-emergence of a form, require evidence of identical ancestry — functional or morphological similarity alone is insufficient to claim identical species reappearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity of groups through descent
rubrics_metrics.description: Groups (genera, families) "follow the same general rules in their appearance and disappearance as do single species... A group does not reappear after it has once disappeared; or its existence, as long as it lasts, is continuous."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use descent and continuity of lineages to interpret group-level fossil ranges: members of a group imply an unbroken succession of generations maintaining that group over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gradual increase and decrease in group diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The general rule is "a gradual increase in number, till the group reaches its maximum, and then, sooner or later, it gradually decreases."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect taxa to show slow, progressive diversification (branching) and eventual tapering/extinction rather than instantaneous peaks; apparent abruptness should be scrutinized for sampling or correlation errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction tied to natural selection and production of improved forms
rubrics_metrics.description: On the theory of natural selection the extinction of old forms and the production of new and improved forms are "intimately connected together."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining extinctions, consider competitive displacement by newly arisen, better-adapted varieties/species as a primary mechanism alongside other causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed law for species duration
rubrics_metrics.description: "No fixed law seems to determine the length of time during which any single species or any single genus endures."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid assuming predictable lifespans for taxa; longevity varies widely and is contingent on numerous factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction often slower than origination
rubrics_metrics.description: There is reason to believe that "the complete extinction of the species of a group is generally a slower process than their production"; the fossil record line "is found to taper more gradually at its upper end... than at its lower end."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When interpreting stratigraphic ranges, expect origination events to appear more abrupt than extinctions; apparent sudden disappearances may be due to record gaps or slower tapering processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity as precursor to extinction
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rarity precedes extinction; and we know that this has been the progress of events with those animals which have been exterminated, either locally or wholly, through man's agency."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observed declines and rarity in populations as warnings of impending extinction; identify likely unfavourable conditions even if specifics are obscure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage causes replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory is grounded on the belief that each new variety/species "is produced and maintained by having some advantage over those with which it comes into competition; and the consequent extinction of less-favoured forms almost inevitably follows."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate proposed replacements of taxa by testing for adaptive advantages in the proposed successor forms relative to incumbents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competition strongest among most similar forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "The competition will generally be most severe... between the forms which are most like each other in all respects."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect closest competition and replacement dynamics among nearest morphological/ ecological relatives; patterns of extinction should often preferentially affect close relatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refugia and isolation preserve taxa
rubrics_metrics.description: A few sufferers may long be preserved "from being fitted to some peculiar line of life, or from inhabiting some distant and isolated station, where they have escaped severe competition."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When taxa persist despite widespread replacement elsewhere, investigate niche specialization or geographic isolation as explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent sudden exterminations can be artefacts or rapid invasions
rubrics_metrics.description: Sudden extermination of whole families or orders (e.g., Trilobites, Ammonites) may result from "probable wide intervals of time between our consecutive formations" or from "sudden immigration or by unusually rapid development" of competitors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat claims of instantaneous mass extinctions with caution: assess completeness of stratigraphic record and possible rapid biotic invasions as alternative explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallel (near-simultaneous) change of marine forms worldwide
rubrics_metrics.description: Scarcely any palæontological discovery is more striking than "the fact, that the forms of life change almost simultaneously throughout the world," especially for marine fossils where successive formations present "an unmistakeable degree of resemblance."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use global parallelism of marine faunas as evidence for broad, non-local causes or general laws governing faunal succession; be cautious about expecting exact species identity across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less strict parallelism for terrestrial/freshwater forms
rubrics_metrics.description: We have not sufficient data to judge whether land and fresh-water productions "have thus changed" in the same parallel manner; terrestrial productions may show less strict degree of parallel succession than marine ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between marine and terrestrial records when correlating faunal stages; expect greater regional variation and asynchronous change on land.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dominant/widely diffused species produce more new varieties
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants (and by extension animals) which are "dominant, varying, and far-spreading" have "produced the greatest number of new varieties."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When predicting centers of origination or diversification, focus on taxa that are abundant, widespread, and variable; dominance and broad range increase likelihood of speciation and formation of new forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diffusion/spread explains global similarity in succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Dominant species spreading from any region "would naturally oftenest give rise to new varieties or incipient species" in other regions; over time dominant forms will prevail everywhere causing parallel succession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret similar faunal stages across continents as possibly resulting from slow diffusion of dominant taxa combined with local variation, rather than identical local origins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing offsets between regions affect species correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: When formations are deposited in two regions during nearly, but not exactly the same period, we should find the same general succession but "the species would not exactly correspond; for there will have been a little more time in the one region than in the other for modification, extinction, and immigration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Correlate formations with attention to possible small temporal offsets; expect species-level differences even when higher-level succession aligns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinct and living species fall into one natural system
rubrics_metrics.description: Extinct and living species "all fall into one grand natural system; and this fact is at once explained on the principle of descent."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use classification and systematic affinities combining fossils and extant taxa as support for common descent; fossils often fill gaps between living groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Older fossils tend to differ more from living forms
rubrics_metrics.description: "The more ancient any form is, the more, as a general rule, it differs from living forms."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing morphological disparity, interpret greater difference as plausibly correlated with greater geological age, while allowing for exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fossils can be intermediate in system but not perfectly intermediate in all characters
rubrics_metrics.description: If 'intermediate' means directly intermediate in all characters the objection is valid; but in natural classification many fossil species "would have to stand between living species" and be intermediate only in some characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claims that fossils are 'missing links' by expecting partial/intermittent intermediacy (some characters linking groups) rather than perfect mosaics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incomplete record limits expectations of filled gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we possess only the last volume of the geological record "and that in a very broken condition, we have no right to expect, except in very rare cases, to fill up wide intervals in the natural system."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conservative in expecting continuous transitional series; use available fossil evidence cautiously and avoid overinterpreting gaps as contradictions of descent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Successive faunas are intermediate in general character
rubrics_metrics.description: On the theory of descent... "the fauna of any great period in the earth’s history will be intermediate in general character between that which preceded and that which succeeded it," subject to extinction, immigration, and unequal intervals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing faunas across successive geological periods, expect general intermediate character at the community level and explain deviations by extinction, immigration, or unequal time intervals between deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Divergence of characters depends on opportunities (niches)
rubrics_metrics.description: Divergence of character "depends solely on the descendants from a species being thus enabled to seize on many and different places in the economy of nature."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret morphological divergence as a consequence of access to diverse ecological opportunities; lack of niche diversification can explain long-term morphological stasis.
